title: Quickstart
content:
Install the SDK, define a pipeline, and run it locally in under five minutes.
A pipeline connects a source to a sink through zero or more transforms. This
page walks through reading a CSV file and loading it into a local DuckDB table,
then points at the deployment guide for anything beyond your laptop.

title: Installation
content:
Quorva supports Python 3.11 through 3.13. Install the base package with
`pip install quorva`. Connector extras are installed per backend, for example
`pip install 'quorva[postgres]'` or `quorva[s3]`. The CLI ships with the base
package. Pin the minor version in production; the on-disk checkpoint format is
stable within a minor release.

title: Architecture overview
content:
A Quorva pipeline is a directed graph of stages executed by the runner. Sources
produce records, transforms map or filter them, and sinks write them out.
Stages exchange records through bounded buffers owned by the runner. State --
offsets, watermarks, and in-flight batches -- is tracked per stage and persisted
by the state store between runs.

title: CLI overview
content:
The `quorva` command wraps the common lifecycle: `quorva validate` checks a
pipeline file, `quorva run` executes it locally, `quorva deploy` submits it to
a runner fleet, and `quorva status` reports on running pipelines. Every
subcommand takes `--config` to point at a quorva.yaml other than the one in the
working directory.

title: Metrics and logging
content:
The runner exports per-stage counters (records in, records out, bytes written,
retries attempted) and timing histograms over a Prometheus endpoint. Logs are
structured JSON by default; set `log_format: text` for human-readable output.
Correlate a record's path through the pipeline with the `trace_id` field
stamped at the source.

title: Troubleshooting common failures
content:
Start with `quorva status --verbose`, which reports each stage's last error and
restart count. A pipeline that starts and then stalls is usually waiting on a
slow sink or an exhausted connection pool. A pipeline that fails at startup is
usually a configuration problem: run `quorva validate` and read the first
error, not the last.

title: Writing transforms
content:
A transform is a Python callable registered with `@qv.transform`. It receives a
batch of records and returns the transformed batch; raising drops the batch
into the retry path. Keep transforms pure -- the runner may re-execute a batch
after a recovery, and a transform with side effects will repeat them.

title: Sources overview
content:
Built-in sources include files (CSV, JSONL, Parquet), object stores, relational
databases via change-data-capture, and HTTP polling. Every source implements
offset tracking so the runner can resume from the last committed position.
Custom sources subclass `qv.Source` and implement `read_batch` and
`current_offset`.

title: Sinks overview
content:
Built-in sinks cover object stores, relational databases, and webhooks. Sinks
declare whether writes are idempotent; the runner uses the declaration to
decide what it may safely retry after a failure. Custom sinks subclass
`qv.Sink` and implement `write_batch`.

title: Glossary
content:
**DLQ** -- dead-letter queue; where records that exhaust their retries are
routed. **QPS** -- queries per second; used when talking about API rate
limits. **Watermark** -- the timestamp up to which a source's input is
considered complete. **Runner** -- the process that executes pipeline stages.
**Offset** -- a source's resumable position in its input.

title: Checkpointing pipeline state
content:
The runner persists each stage's offsets and watermarks to the state store at
every commit interval. After a crash or redeploy, the pipeline resumes from the
last committed state instead of reprocessing its input from the beginning.
Point the state store at durable storage with the `checkpoint_store_uri` key in
quorva.yaml; the default commit interval is 30 seconds, tunable per pipeline
with `commit_interval_s`.

title: QRV-4012: sink write rejected
content:
Raised when a sink rejects a batch because the record schema does not match the
destination's declared schema. Common causes: a column added upstream that the
destination table lacks, or a type widening (int to float) the destination
refuses. The failing batch is routed to dead-letter handling if configured;
otherwise the pipeline stops. Fix the destination schema or add a transform
that projects the record onto the destination's columns, then resume the run.

title: Error code index
content:
QRV-1001 invalid pipeline file. QRV-1002 unknown stage name. QRV-2003 source
connection refused. QRV-2004 source credentials rejected. QRV-3001 transform
raised. QRV-3002 transform timeout. QRV-4010 sink connection refused. QRV-4011
sink credentials rejected. QRV-4012 sink write rejected. QRV-4013 sink
timeout. QRV-5001 state store unavailable. QRV-5002 checkpoint corrupt.

title: PostgresSink API reference
content:
`qv.sinks.PostgresSink(dsn, table, *, flush_interval_ms=250, batch_rows=500,
idempotent=True)`. Buffered rows are flushed when either `batch_rows` is
reached or `flush_interval_ms` elapses, whichever comes first; the default
flush interval is 250 milliseconds. `idempotent=True` declares writes safe to
retry, which lets the runner re-submit a batch after a transient failure.

title: quorva.yaml reference
content:
Top-level keys: `name` -- pipeline name, required. `runner` -- local or fleet.
`checkpoint_store_uri` -- where pipeline state is persisted; accepts file://,
s3://, or postgres:// URIs. `commit_interval_s` -- how often state is
committed, default 30. `log_format` -- json or text. `on_error` -- stop,
skip, or dead-letter. Connector credentials do not belong here; see the
authentication guides.

title: Backpressure and flow control
content:
When a downstream stage cannot keep up, the runner slows the stages feeding it
rather than letting buffers grow without bound. Each buffer has a high-water
mark; when it fills, upstream stages pause until the consumer drains it below
the low-water mark. This applies end to end: a slow destination ultimately
pauses the source itself, so memory stays bounded no matter how fast the input
arrives.

title: Delivery guarantees
content:
Quorva provides effectively-once delivery: each record's effect reaches the
destination a single time, even across crashes and restarts. The runner
commits source offsets and sink acknowledgments together; after a failure it
resumes from the last committed state, and re-submits only batches the sink
never acknowledged. Sinks that declare idempotent writes make the re-submission
safe; for the rest, the runner uses a transactional two-phase commit where the
backend supports it.

title: Dead-letter handling
content:
A record that keeps failing -- its batch has exhausted the retry policy -- is
routed to the pipeline's dead-letter destination instead of stopping the run.
Configure it with `on_error: dead-letter` and a `dead_letter_uri` pointing at a
file, object-store prefix, or table. Each routed record carries the original
payload, the failing stage, the final error, and the attempt count, so the
batch can be inspected and replayed later with `quorva replay`.

title: Authenticating with OAuth service accounts
content:
Create a service account in the Quorva console, grant it the pipeline-runner
role, and download its client credentials. Reference the credentials file from
the connector, or exchange it yourself: POST the client id and secret to
`/oauth/token` and pass the returned bearer token in the `Authorization`
header. Tokens expire after one hour; the SDK refreshes them automatically
before expiry.

title: Changelog
content:
2.3.1 -- fixed OAuth token refresh racing a concurrent request; OAuth errors
now carry the provider response. 2.3.0 -- OAuth support for the webhook sink;
deprecated implicit OAuth flow; OAuth client credentials may be rotated
without restart. 2.2.4 -- OAuth token cache no longer written world-readable.
2.2.3 -- retry jitter made configurable. 2.2.2 -- OAuth scopes documented per
connector. 2.2.1 -- fixed OAuth redirect on the console login page.

title: Retry policy
content:
Transient failures are retried per stage with exponential backoff: `retries:
{max_attempts: 5, base_delay_ms: 100, max_delay_ms: 30000, jitter: true}`.
Only failures the connector marks retryable are attempted again; a schema
rejection is not, a timeout is. A batch that exhausts its attempts is handed
to dead-letter handling when configured. Tune `max_attempts` down for
latency-sensitive pipelines rather than disabling retries outright.

title: API index
content:
qv.RetryPolicy. qv.retry.backoff_full_jitter. qv.retry.backoff_equal_jitter.
qv.Source.retry_hints. qv.Sink.retryable_errors. qv.errors.RetryExhausted.
qv.errors.RetryableError. qv.testing.FlakySink (simulates retryable failures).
qv.transform. qv.Pipeline. qv.sinks.PostgresSink. qv.sinks.S3Sink.
qv.sources.S3Source. qv.execute.

title: Schema validation
content:
Enable validation on a source with `schema: {mode: enforce, ref:
schemas/orders.json}`. In `enforce` mode a non-conforming record fails its
batch; in `warn` mode it is counted and logged but passed through. Schemas are
JSON Schema draft 2020-12; the reference may point at a file or an inline
definition. Validation runs before the first transform, so transforms can rely
on the declared shape.

title: Frequently asked questions
content:
Is schema validation available on the free tier? Contact your account team.
Does schema validation affect billing? See the pricing page. Can schema
validation be enabled per environment? Reach out to support with your org id.
Where do I report a schema validation bug? The issue tracker. Is there a
schema validation roadmap? Watch the public milestones page.

title: Authenticating with API keys
Batching and throughput
content:
Throughput is mostly a function of batch size. Each sink declares a sweet spot
(`batch_rows` on the relational sinks, `batch_bytes` on the object-store
sinks); start there and double it until p99 write latency degrades. Larger
batches amortize per-request overhead but raise retry cost, since a failed
batch is retried whole. The runner's per-stage `records out` counter divided
by wall time is the number to watch.

title: Rate limits
content:
The ingest API accepts 1,000 requests per second per organization, measured
over a sliding ten-second window; bursts above the limit receive HTTP 429 with
a Retry-After header. Pipeline traffic through connectors is not subject to
this limit -- it applies to the REST ingest endpoint only. Contact support to
raise the ceiling for sustained high-volume ingest.

title: S3 sink
content:
`qv.sinks.S3Sink(bucket, prefix, *, format="parquet", batch_bytes=64_000_000)`
writes pipeline output to an S3 bucket as size-bounded objects under the given
prefix. Object names embed the stage, window, and batch sequence so a replay
overwrites rather than duplicates. Formats: parquet, jsonl, csv. Credentials
come from the standard provider chain or the connector's `credentials` block.

title: S3 source
content:
`qv.sources.S3Source(bucket, prefix, *, format="auto")` reads objects from an
S3 bucket into the pipeline, tracking the last fully-read object as its
offset. New objects under the prefix are picked up on each poll. Use the
`since` parameter to skip historical objects on first run. Formats are
inferred from object suffixes unless pinned.

title: Running pipelines (v1)
content:
In Quorva v1, construct a `Pipeline` and call its `run()` method:
`Pipeline(source, transforms, sink).run(blocking=True)`. `run()` takes
`blocking`, `max_records`, and `state_dir`. The v1 API is maintained for the
1.x line but receives no new features; new projects should start on v2.

title: Executing pipelines (v2)
content:
Quorva v2 replaces the method call with a module-level entry point:
`qv.execute(pipeline, *, wait=True, limit=None, state_uri=None)`. `wait`
replaces v1's `blocking`, `limit` replaces `max_records`, and `state_uri`
generalizes `state_dir` to any checkpoint store URI. `qv.execute` returns a
`RunHandle` with `status()`, `wait()`, and `cancel()`.

title: Migrating from v1 to v2
content:
Replace `Pipeline(...).run(...)` with `qv.execute(Pipeline(...), ...)`:
`blocking` becomes `wait`, `max_records` becomes `limit`, and `state_dir`
becomes `state_uri` (prefix the old path with `file://`). `run()` returned
None; `qv.execute` returns a RunHandle, so code that polled logs for completion
can call `wait()` instead. The v1 method keeps working under 2.x with a
deprecation warning until 3.0.

title: Ephemeral runs: executing without persisted state
content:
For backfills and tests where resuming is pointless, disable state persistence
entirely: pass `state_uri=None` to `qv.execute`, or set `checkpoint_store_uri:
none` in quorva.yaml. The runner keeps offsets in memory for the life of the
process and writes nothing to the state store; a crash means the run starts
over. Combine with `limit` to bound reprocessing.

title: Supplying credentials from the environment
content:
Connectors resolve credentials from the process environment before reading any
file: set `QUORVA_API_KEY`, or for OAuth `QUORVA_CLIENT_ID` and
`QUORVA_CLIENT_SECRET`. On fleet runners, workload identity is preferred: the
runner exchanges its platform identity for a Quorva token at startup, and no
secret is written to configuration or disk at all.

title: Deploying with the CLI
content:
`quorva deploy pipeline.yaml --fleet prod` validates the pipeline, uploads it,
and starts it on the named fleet. `--watch` tails the rollout; `--dry-run`
stops after validation. The CLI reads fleet credentials from your console
session (`quorva login`). Roll back with `quorva deploy --revision N`.

title: Programmatic deployment
content:
Fleets expose a REST deployment endpoint for CI systems and anything else that
cannot shell out: PUT the rendered pipeline definition to
`/fleets/{fleet}/pipelines/{name}` with a service-account bearer token. The
response carries the revision number; GET the same path for rollout status.
The SDK wraps this as `qv.fleet.deploy(pipeline, fleet=...)`.

title: quorva validate
content:
`quorva validate pipeline.yaml` parses the pipeline file, resolves every stage
name against the registry, type-checks the source/transform/sink wiring, and
reports the first error with its line. It makes no network calls and touches
no state, so it is safe to run in CI. A clean validate is a precondition the
runner re-checks at startup anyway.

title: quorva run (local execution)
content:
`quorva run pipeline.yaml` executes a pipeline on the local machine, in the
current process, with no fleet involved. It is the inner-loop command: fast to
start, logs to the terminal, and honours `--limit` and `--state-uri`. Use it
for development and backfills; `quorva deploy` is for putting a pipeline on a
runner fleet in production.

title: quorva status
content:
`quorva status` lists running pipelines and, with `--verbose`, each stage's
last error, restart count, and current offset. It reads the fleet's control
plane, not the data plane, so it is cheap to poll. For per-stage record counts
and timing, see the metrics endpoint rather than status.

title: Environment-variable overrides
content:
Any quorva.yaml scalar can be overridden from the environment with the
`QUORVA_` prefix and the uppercased dotted path: `QUORVA_COMMIT_INTERVAL_S=10`
overrides `commit_interval_s`. Overrides are read once at startup. This is for
deployment-specific values; connector credentials have their own resolution
order (environment, then file, then workload identity).

title: Defining a pipeline
content:
A pipeline is declared in quorva.yaml as a `source`, an ordered list of
`transforms`, and one or more `sinks`, or built in Python by composing
`qv.Source`, `qv.transform` callables, and `qv.Sink` objects. The runner wires
them into a stage graph. Every pipeline needs a unique `name`, used for state
scoping and status reporting.

title: The record model
content:
Records are plain dictionaries with JSON-compatible values plus a small
envelope the runner stamps: a `trace_id` set at the source, the source offset,
and the arrival timestamp. Transforms see the payload; the envelope travels
alongside. Keep payloads flat where you can -- deeply nested records cost more
to serialize between stages.

title: Batches and buffers
content:
Stages exchange records in batches through bounded buffers owned by the runner.
Batch size is a per-sink tuning knob, not a global; buffers have high- and
low-water marks that drive flow control. A batch is the unit of retry and of
dead-lettering: a failure routes the whole batch, not a single record.

title: Connectors
content:
Connectors are the installable source and sink backends. Install the ones you
need as extras: `pip install 'quorva[postgres,s3]'`. Each connector declares
its capabilities -- offset tracking for sources, write idempotency for sinks --
which the runner reads to decide what it may safely retry or resume.

title: CSV source
content:
`qv.sources.CsvSource(path, *, has_header=True, delimiter=",")` reads rows from
a CSV file or glob into records keyed by column name. Offsets are byte
positions, so a run resumes mid-file after a restart. Large files stream; they
are not loaded whole.

title: JSONL source
content:
`qv.sources.JsonlSource(path)` reads newline-delimited JSON, one record per
line, with the line number as offset. Malformed lines route to dead-letter
handling when configured rather than stopping the run.

title: Parquet source
content:
`qv.sources.ParquetSource(path)` reads Parquet row groups into records. It is
the fastest file source for columnar data and preserves types without the
inference CSV needs. Offsets are (file, row-group) pairs.

title: HTTP polling source
content:
`qv.sources.HttpSource(url, *, interval_s=60, cursor_param="since")` polls an
HTTP endpoint on an interval and emits the returned items, advancing a cursor
it passes back on the next poll. Use it for APIs without a streaming feed.

title: Webhook sink
content:
`qv.sinks.WebhookSink(url, *, method="POST", idempotent=False)` posts each
batch to an HTTP endpoint. Because most webhooks are not idempotent, the runner
will not retry a webhook write by default; declare `idempotent=True` only if
the endpoint de-duplicates.

title: DuckDB sink
content:
`qv.sinks.DuckDbSink(path, table)` writes pipeline output to a local DuckDB
file -- the default sink in the quickstart because it needs no server. Writes
are transactional per batch, so they are safe to retry.

title: BigQuery sink
content:
`qv.sinks.BigQuerySink(dataset, table, *, idempotent=True)` streams rows into
BigQuery using insert IDs for de-duplication, which is what makes its writes
idempotent and therefore retryable by the runner.

title: Testing pipelines
content:
`qv.testing` provides `MemorySource` and `MemorySink` for wiring a pipeline
against in-memory data, and `FlakySink`, which fails a configurable fraction of
batches to exercise retry and dead-letter paths. Tests run the pipeline with
`qv.execute(..., state_uri=None)` so no state is persisted.

title: Local development loop
content:
The fast loop is edit, `quorva validate`, `quorva run --limit 1000` against a
sample, read the terminal logs. Keep a small fixture file next to the pipeline
so a run needs no network. Switch the sink to DuckDB locally and to the real
destination only in the deployed config.

title: Deploying to a fleet
content:
A runner fleet is a pool of worker processes managed by the control plane.
`quorva deploy` uploads a validated pipeline and schedules it; the fleet
assigns stages to workers, restarts failed stages, and exposes status and
metrics. Fleets scale horizontally -- add workers to run more pipelines, not to
make one stage faster.

title: Security model
content:
Quorva holds no long-lived secrets of its own: connector credentials come from
the process environment, a referenced file, or workload identity on fleet
runners. Pipeline definitions are not secret and may be committed; the values
they reference are resolved at runtime and never written into state or logs.

title: Versioning and compatibility
content:
Quorva follows semantic versioning. The on-disk checkpoint format is stable
within a minor release; a major release may change it and ships a migration
note. The Python API's v1 surface is maintained through the 1.x line; v2 is the
current surface. Pin the minor version in production.

title: Performance basics
content:
Throughput is governed by the slowest stage and by batch size at the sinks;
latency by the commit interval and buffer depth. Measure with the per-stage
counters before tuning. Scaling workers helps when stages are independent; it
does nothing for a single saturated sink, which wants a larger batch instead.

title: Glossary (extended)
content:
**CDC** -- change data capture; reading a database's commit log as a stream.
**2PC** -- two-phase commit; a protocol for atomic writes across systems.
**RPS** -- requests per second, used interchangeably with QPS for rate limits.
**Tail latency** -- high-percentile (p95/p99) latency, the slow requests.
**Backfill** -- reprocessing historical input, usually as an ephemeral run.

title: QRV-5002: checkpoint corrupt
content:
Raised at startup when the state store holds a checkpoint the runner cannot
parse -- usually a checkpoint written by a different Quorva minor version, or a
partially-written file left by a killed process. The run refuses to start
rather than reprocess from an unknown position. Resolve by pointing
`checkpoint_store_uri` at a fresh location to start clean, or restoring a known
-good checkpoint; there is no in-place repair.

title: Record ordering
content:
Within a single source partition, records keep their arrival order all the way
to the sink: the runner does not reorder a stage's output. Across partitions
there is no global order -- two records from different partitions may be written
in either sequence. Transforms that need to compare neighbouring records should
rely on the within-partition guarantee, not on a global one.

title: Parallelism
content:
The runner assigns each stage a number of workers; raising a stage's worker
count lets independent batches run at the same time. This helps only when the
stage is the bottleneck and its work is divisible -- a single downstream sink
that serializes writes gains nothing from more upstream workers. Set worker
counts from the per-stage throughput counters, not by guessing.

title: Idempotent writes
content:
A sink is idempotent when applying the same batch twice has the same effect as
applying it once -- achieved with insert IDs, upserts on a key, or a
transactional commit. The runner only retries writes a sink declares
idempotent; for the rest it uses a two-phase commit where the backend allows,
and otherwise routes an uncertain batch to dead-letter rather than risk a
duplicate.

title: Performance tuning FAQ
content:
Does a larger batch size improve write throughput for the Postgres sink? It
depends. Does batch size affect latency as well as throughput? Yes, indirectly.
Can I change the batch size per environment? See configuration. Is there a
recommended batch size for high-throughput Postgres writes? Contact support.
Why did my write throughput drop after I increased batch size? Open an issue.

title: Authentication FAQ
content:
How do I authenticate the webhook sink with an API key? See the connector docs.
Can the webhook sink use an API key and OAuth together? No. Where does the
webhook sink read the API key from? The credentials block. Does an API key for
the webhook sink expire? Keys do not expire. Is the webhook sink API key

title: Deployment FAQ
content:
Do I need to validate the pipeline configuration before deploying? The runner
re-validates. Can I deploy without validating the pipeline configuration first?
Not recommended. Where is the pipeline configuration validated before deploy?
In CI and at startup. What validates the pipeline configuration on deploy? The
control plane. Is deploy-time configuration validation strict? Yes.

title: Postgres source (CDC)
content:
`qv.sources.PostgresSource(dsn, *, slot, tables)` streams a Postgres database's
changes into the pipeline by reading its logical-replication slot -- inserts,
updates and deletes as they commit. Its offset is the log position, so a run
resumes without re-reading the table. This is for ingesting *from* Postgres;
writing pipeline output *to* Postgres is the Postgres sink.

title: Configuring sinks (v1)
content:
In Quorva v1 a sink is attached by calling `pipeline.add_sink(sink)` after
construction; multiple calls add multiple sinks, applied in call order. The
`add_sink` method is maintained on the 1.x line but is not available in v2,
where sinks are attached with the `.to(...)` operator instead.

title: Attaching sinks (v2)
content:
Quorva v2 replaces `add_sink()` with the `.to(...)` operator:
`pipeline.to(sink_a).to(sink_b)` attaches sinks left to right, returning the
pipeline so calls chain. `.to()` exists only in v2; v1 code using `add_sink`
keeps working under 2.x with a deprecation warning until 3.0.
